title: What not to put on the site for a community sports club
metaTitle: What to cut from a sports club site
excerpt: Cut the trophy case and the pages nobody maintains. Keep people playing, a way to start, and a clear path to membership or the schedule.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground. A view with the extra noise removed, which is the edit a club site needs.
caption: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove from a club site?
faqs.answer: Remove the trophy case from the lead, including its quieter costumes: a president's letter, a sponsor mosaic above the timetable, a drone film of the building. Move pride to a season page. Leave one true line about the league if a serious player needs it.

faqs.question: Which pages should stay?
faqs.answer: Keep play and how to start, the sessions in member language, fees with the shape visible, a phone-readable schedule, named coaches, and a contact path with a reply time you keep. Safeguarding stays as itself, linked and dated. That set is enough for someone deciding whether to join.

faqs.question: Why is a shorter site easier to trust?
faqs.answer: Every extra page can go stale by November, when the volunteer who loved the launch is back to coaching. A short site has owners and a chance of matching Tuesday. Length is not the same thing as care.

markdown:
Community sports club website mistakes often start with a trophy case on the homepage. It reassures the committee and confuses a person deciding whether to join. Keep people playing, how to start, and a clear way to see membership or the schedule. A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long site that performs taste.

The cut is an editorial decision. Every block you remove makes the remaining blocks easier to believe, because the visitor can finish them.

## The trophy case, in all its costumes

The obvious version is a wall of cups, a slider of finals, and a headline about a winning tradition. The quieter versions do the same job. A president's letter about heritage. A sponsor mosaic above the timetable. A drone shot of the building set to music. A row of values with no session attached. Each one is the club talking to itself.

Move pride to a place that has earned it. A season review, linked from the footer, can hold the photograph of the squad and the year. Members who want it will open it. Prospects who need Tuesday will not have to climb over it. One line on the homepage can mention that teams play in named leagues, if that fact helps a serious player choose. The line is enough.

Google's guide to [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the page exists for an audience who would find it useful if they came directly, and whether they can leave having done what they came to do. It also warns against writing to a word count you heard a search engine prefers. A club site padded with history, so that it looks substantial, fails both tests. The audience came to see if they can play. Substance is the schedule, the fee, and the people in the room.

Apply the same test to a "gallery" that is only celebrations. If the pictures never show a beginner, the gallery is a trophy case with a friendlier name. Replace the set, or park it under a season page.

## Pages that belong in a folder

Minutes, constitutions, and old AGM packs matter to a committee and almost never to a first visit. Keep them available for members and for anyone doing due diligence. Place them behind a clear footer link called Club documents. Do not give each PDF a turn in the main menu, and do not paste their prose onto the homepage in the name of transparency.

Stale news is a cousin of the folder problem. A front page that leads with a post about a tournament from two seasons ago tells the visitor the site is unattended, which they generalize to the club. If you cannot write news monthly, stop having a news river. Let the schedule be the living page. A single "this week" note, maintained by the same person who updates the times, is plenty.

Duplicate explanations should go. If fees are correct on the fees page, the homepage should link there rather than paraphrase a number that will drift. Two prices for one membership is a trust problem you can prevent by having one home for the figure. The same rule covers ages, trial rules, and the address. One source, linked everywhere else.

Generic wellbeing claims, unsupported partnership badges, and stock photographs of other sports are cuts even when a volunteer meant well. They are taste performing as content. The visitor cannot join a stock photograph.

## What stays, in order

Keep a homepage that shows people playing and how to start. Keep the sessions, named in member language, each with an outcome and a boundary. Keep fees with the shape visible: the number, the period, what is in, what is out. Keep the schedule readable on a phone. Keep coaches named. Keep a short contact path with a true reply time. Keep the map and the door to use.

That set is a complete site for a person deciding whether to join. It can fit in a handful of pages. A club with juniors and seniors can still be brief if each offer is a block on a menu rather than a microsite. Add a page when an offer has its own rules, its own timetable, and a real owner. Refuse a page whose only purpose is to make the menu look more like a company.

Ballarat Box Sports is a public Hanabi example of a community sports brand site. The lesson for a cut-down site is that a point of view does not require a long site. A clear activity, honest pictures, and a way in can carry a brand. Length is not the same thing as care.

Policies that the law or your governing body expects, such as safeguarding, stay. They stay as themselves, linked and dated, written so a parent can find the welfare contact. Keeping a policy is different from leading with it. The lead remains the session.

## Taste is a weak reason to add a block

A block often survives because it looks like the sites the committee admires. A journal. A manifesto. A full-bleed quote. An animated counter of "members since." Admiration is not a job. Ask what the visitor can do after seeing the block that they could not do before. If the answer is only "feel something," check whether the photograph of play already did that job.

Counters are a special temptation because they look like evidence. A counter of founded-years, or of social followers, rarely helps someone choose a Tuesday. If you have a true, useful number, write it in a sentence. "Junior sessions are capped at sixteen so each child is coached." That sentence is evidence. A spinning number is a costume.

Music, cursors, and intro animations are taste as well. They delay the schedule. On a phone in a public place they can be embarrassing, which is a cruel way to introduce a club. Let the page be still unless motion shows something, such as a timetable filtering to tonight. Even then, honor reduced motion.

The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) are a useful brake on taste. Content should be perceivable and operable. A menu that only appears on hover, a schedule that is text baked into a photograph, a video with no way to reach the fee: these are aesthetic choices that remove the site from some of the people you say you welcome. Cut them in favor of text, buttons, and real headings.

## A shorter site is easier to keep true

Every extra page is a page that can go stale. A short site has a chance of matching reality in November, when the volunteer who loved the launch has gone back to coaching. Assign an owner to each remaining page. Schedule, fees, sessions, coaches, contact. If a page has no owner, it is a candidate to cut.

Review the site at the start of the term with a simple read-through on a phone. Could a stranger start. Are the prices current. Are the coaches still the coaches. Does any trophy block sit above the door. Fix those, and ignore the urge to add a new section because a neighboring club added one.

Hanabi's work on sites like this is the same editorial habit. Decide what the first screen must prove, then remove what argues with it. The studio designs and builds. The club still has to tell the truth about Tuesday. No page can substitute for that.

When the remaining pages are the true ones, look at them as a set. The homepage promises play. The fees page shows the shape. The sessions page uses member words. The contact page makes a promise you keep. If one of them drifts back toward a brochure, pull it back. The set is the product.

Read the site as if you had ten seconds and a child in the car. The first tap should be tonight's session or the fee, and the words should be large enough to read without stepping into the shade. If the first tap is a sponsor, a film, or a crest, the cut is not finished.

After the cut, count the pages that still have an owner. If the number is small and each owner can update their page in a week, you have a site. If the number is large and the owners are imaginary, you have a brochure that will drift. Choose the site. Social embeds belong in this count. A feed that shows an empty widget, or a post from a year ago, is a page you are pretending to maintain. Link to the profile in the footer if you want, and let the schedule be the thing that updates.

## The same mistake in a shop window

A club flatters itself with silverware. A consumer brand flatters itself with a manifesto before the object. The visitor is different, and the thing they need to see is different, but the failure rhymes: the organization speaks first, and the buyer cannot find the offer. The next piece applies that test to a shop that sells a physical thing. It is [what the homepage has to prove for a consumer brand](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-consumer-brand).

If you are about to commission a rebuild, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and notice what the first screens refuse to say. Bring your current site and a list of the pages nobody updates.
